Creator Guide

Visual hooks that
stop the scroll

A reference for the kinds of opening frames we want to prioritise in our videos — with real examples you can copy, adapt and improve on.

The hook decides how far your video travelsThe first one to two seconds are what the algorithm actually tests. Same script, same edit, same product — swap a flat opening frame for a strong visual hook and the same video goes from a few thousand views to hundreds of thousands. None of the creators below have a bigger audience than you. They just earned the first second.

Action hooks

Something is physically happening in the first frame. The viewer has to wait to find out how it ends.

The hair straightener series

Our most reliable format right now. Take a hair straightener and press something through it that clearly does not belong there. The reveal at the end is the reason people stay.

Slime, gel and goo are pure sensory bait. Keep the texture in frame and moving — a static blob does nothing.

Object hooks

Nothing needs to happen — the object itself is the hook. Hold it up in frame one and start talking.

Unexpected objects, vegetables and accessories

Pick something the viewer has to look at twice. It should be odd, but still make sense once you explain it.

03

Text hooks

The on-screen title is a hook too. It works together with the visual, not instead of it.

Use emojis — especially urgency emojis

In your video titles, add emojis. Urgency emojis work best because they read as a warning before the viewer has even finished the sentence.

🚨❌❗❓⚠️😲👽
Keep it shortSix to eight words. It has to be readable in one glance.
Place it highTop third of the frame, clear of the platform UI.
One or two emojisMore than that reads as spam and the eye stops parsing it.
04

Interaction hooks

Give people a reason to type. Comments are the cheapest reach you will ever get.

Make a mistake on purpose

People cannot resist correcting us. One deliberate, obvious error is enough — keep it small and clearly wrong, never something that makes the advice useless.

148K views

Getting the subject ranking wrong

Sparks a natural argument in the comments without any call to action.

@estudiaconcata↗
✓

Before you post

Thirty seconds of checking saves a video that would otherwise get buried.

DO

  • Put the strange thing in the very first frame — not at second three.
  • Make sure the hook connects to what the video is actually about.
  • Keep the object large and centred so it reads on a small screen.
  • Give a reveal or payoff at the end, so there is a reason to stay.
  • Shoot in good light — texture and colour are the whole point.

DON’T

  • Don’t go absurd for the sake of it. Random is not the same as unexpected.
  • Don’t bury the hook behind a long intro or a logo.
  • Don’t reuse the exact same hook twice in a row on one account.
  • Don’t let the text cover your face or the object.
  • Don’t make a deliberate mistake that makes the advice wrong or useless.

Keep experimenting. These are examples, not a fixed list. The goal is to find new formats and hooks that really work — if you try something that performs, send it over so we can add it here.

View counts are shown for TikTok. Instagram hides view counts from logged-out visitors, so likes are shown instead — the label on each badge says which.
